hero.name: Boris Sargsyan
hero.tagline: Studying how systems break, so I can help build the ones that don't.
hero.intro: Cybersecurity student at Marist University, originally from Yerevan, Armenia, and a recent IB Diploma graduate of UWC Dilijan. Before university I built and shipped real things as like a custom software platform for a student-run, charity based business, a fleet of FPV drones designed and flown from scratch, and 15+ completed programming courses across Python, Java, C/C++, JavaScript, and SQL.

about.heading: About
paragraphs:
I'm a cybersecurity student at Marist University. My path here started at UWC Dilijan, where I completed the IB Diploma while building things on the side as like a full operations platform for a student-run business, a self-built fleet of FPV drones, and a stack of self-directed courses in Python, Java, C/C++, JavaScript, and SQL.

Outside the classroom, I compete as an Armenian national Taekwondo champion and hold a 1st Dan black belt, the same discipline that now drives how I approach learning security from the ground up. I'm currently working through foundational ethical hacking and network security material and looking for an internship where I can put it to use on a real team.

research.title: How Vulnerable Is a Home Router? A Penetration Testing Study Using Wireshark
research.description: Ran a controlled, passive penetration test on a home router's default configuration using Wireshark, capturing and analyzing traffic across three attack surfaces: an HTTP login test that exposed credentials in cleartext, a DNS lookup test that revealed browsing activity despite HTTPS, and an ARP test that exposed the network's exposure to man-in-the-middle spoofing. Concluded that most consumer routers ship with these protections off by default.

research.title: How Does Increasing Password Length Affect the Time Required for a Brute-Force Attack Under Different Processing Speeds?
research.description: Built a mathematical model (T = N^L / R) comparing brute-force cracking time across CPU, GPU, multi-GPU, and theoretical quantum processing speeds, then used logarithmic linearization to show that password length — not attacker hardware — is the dominant factor in cracking resistance, holding even under quantum-scale guess rates.
